channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [22] Defeating fear with exposure therapy delivered by mental health nurses in primary care for anxiety disorders in older adults: a protocol for a cluster-randomized controlled trial (DeFEAD65+).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study is a protocol for a cluster-randomised controlled trial (cRCT) investigating whether exposure therapy (ET) delivered by mental health nurses (MHNs) in primary care is more (cost-)effective than usual care for reducing anxiety symptoms and improving quality of life in older adults (65+) with anxiety disorders. The trial aims to address the under-treatment of anxiety disorders in this population, where pharmacotherapy is often preferred despite risks and patient preferences for psychotherapy.
FINDINGS: The trial will randomise primary care centres to either ET (8 sessions over 12 weeks) or usual care, with a one-year follow-up. Primary outcomes include anxiety severity (Geriatric Anxiety Inventory), societal costs (TiC-P), and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L). Secondary outcomes include comorbid depressive symptoms and disorder-specific anxiety symptoms. Predictors, moderators, and mechanisms of change will also be explored. Sample size and effect sizes are not yet reported, as this is a protocol.
INTERPRETATION: As a protocol, this study has not yet produced results, so no conclusions can be drawn about efficacy or effectiveness. The design (cRCT) is appropriate for evaluating interventions delivered at the cluster level (primary care centres) and avoids contamination between groups. However, external validity will depend on the representativeness of the primary care centres and participants recruited. The study’s focus on ET delivered by MHNs is innovative and could address a significant treatment gap if proven effective. Results are eagerly awaited.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study could change practice if ET delivered by MHNs in primary care is found to be (cost-)effective, offering an alternative to pharmacotherapy for older adults with anxiety disorders. Clinicians should await the trial results before considering implementation, as current evidence is preliminary.

item.title: [20] Acupuncture for Symptoms Characteristic of the Fatigue-Sleep Disturbance-Depression Symptom Cluster (FSDSC) in Breast Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether acupuncture or acupressure reduces fatigue, sleep disturbance/insomnia, and depression—symptoms that often co-occur in breast cancer patients (the fatigue-sleep disturbance-depression symptom cluster, FSDSC). Twenty-one randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 2,153 participants were synthesized.
FINDINGS: Meta-analysis showed significant improvements with acupuncture/acupressure versus controls: fatigue (MFI: -9.73; 95% CI, -18.03 to -1.43; p=0.02; BFI: -1.13; 95% CI, -1.79 to -0.47; p=0.0008), sleep quality (PSQI: -2.43; 95% CI, -3.45 to -1.42; p<0.0001) and insomnia severity (ISI: -1.05; 95% CI, -1.74 to -0.36; p=0.003), depression (-1.34; 95% CI, -2.08 to -0.60; p=0.0004), and quality of life (FACT-B: 8.10; 95% CI, 6.47 to 9.72; p<0.0001).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base consists of 21 small-to-moderate-sized RCTs with generally unclear or high risk of bias, limiting certainty. Effect sizes are statistically significant but modest in magnitude (e.g., PSQI reduction of ~2.4 points on a 0–21 scale), and heterogeneity was not fully explored in the abstract. Funding sources and comparator details (e.g., sham acupuncture) were not reported, raising potential bias. Larger, rigorously blinded RCTs with active comparators are needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence suggests acupuncture or acupressure may offer small improvements in fatigue, sleep, depression, and quality of life in breast cancer patients, but the clinical significance is uncertain. Consider as an adjunct option while awaiting higher-quality trials; monitor for placebo effects and ensure integration with standard oncologic and psychiatric care.

item.title: [19] Effects of a sleep program on sleep, performance and health in university students: Study protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a pragmatic randomised controlled trial (RCT) in 118 university students (18–30 y) with chronic insomnia disorder, testing whether a 12-week group-based sleep program (integrating CBT-I, motivational and coping strategies) improves insomnia severity versus wait-list control, with 12-month follow-up.
FINDINGS: The trial is ongoing; no outcome data are reported in the abstract. Planned primary outcome is change in Bergen Insomnia Scale score at 12 weeks and 12 months. Secondary outcomes include subjective/objective sleep measures, mental health, cognition, academic performance, health behaviours, fitness, and biological markers.
INTERPRETATION: As a study protocol, no efficacy results are available; internal validity will depend on randomisation, allocation concealment, blinding of assessors, and attrition rates once published. External validity may be limited to university students with chronic insomnia, but the pragmatic design and long follow-up strengthen generalisability to routine campus health services if effectiveness is demonstrated.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No change in practice yet; if the program proves effective, it could offer a scalable, group-based alternative to individual CBT-I for students, pending cost-effectiveness and implementation data.

item.title: [18] Patterns of antidepressant persistence in mood and anxiety disorders: a retrospective population-based cohort study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective population-based cohort study examined real-world persistence with prescribed antidepressants over 12 months in 76,200 adults with mood or anxiety disorders in Manitoba, Canada, using administrative prescription data from 2015–2021.
FINDINGS: Only 25% of new antidepressant users persisted with their initial prescription at 12 months; 75.4% discontinued within a year. Persistence rates declined from 56% at 3 months to 41% at 6 months, 33% at 9 months, and 25% at 12 months. Lower persistence was associated with male sex (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.84–0.90), younger age <25 years (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.71–0.77), receipt of income assistance (OR 0.57, 95% CI 0.53–0.61), tricyclic antidepressant use (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.28–0.34), concurrent benzodiazepine use (OR 0.88, 95% CI 0.84–0.91), prior PTSD diagnosis (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.76–0.91), and more mood/anxiety ambulatory visits (OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.88–0.95).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is strong in size and consistency due to the large, population-based sample and robust administrative data, but residual confounding and lack of clinical outcomes (e.g., relapse, symptom scores) limit causal inference. The very low 12-month persistence (25%) is clinically meaningful and highlights a gap between guideline recommendations and real-world practice. The identified risk factors can guide targeted interventions, though effect sizes are modest and may not translate directly to improved outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should proactively monitor and support adherence in high-risk groups (e.g., younger patients, those on TCAs or with PTSD), and consider structured follow-up or shared decision-making to improve persistence with antidepressant treatment.

item.title: [14] Trends in Autism Spectrum Disorder Cumulative Incidence and Incidence Density: A Systematic Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review (PRISMA 2020) examined whether rising autism spectrum disorder (ASD) prevalence reflects a true increase in incidence by synthesizing population-based studies of ASD incidence in individuals under 18 years. It distinguished between birth-defined cohorts (Category A) and dynamic annual incidence density studies (Category B), aiming to clarify whether methodological differences explain observed trends.
FINDINGS: Twenty-seven studies were included (14 Category A, 13 Category B). Incidence increased in dynamic populations with moderate or low ascertainment comprehensiveness, particularly for broader ASD categories. However, high-comprehensiveness birth cohort studies (Category A) showed inconsistent patterns and lower male-to-female ratios, suggesting no clear temporal increase in underlying risk.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by methodological heterogeneity and potential biases in ascertainment, diagnostic criteria, and population dynamics. The lack of consistent increases in high-quality birth cohort studies weakens claims of a true "autism epidemic." The findings highlight how administrative and diagnostic factors can inflate incidence estimates in dynamic populations, while more rigorous designs do not support a genuine rise in ASD occurrence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should interpret rising ASD diagnoses cautiously, considering that changes may reflect improved detection or broader diagnostic criteria rather than a true increase in incidence. No immediate clinical practice changes are warranted based on these findings alone.

item.title: [14] Transdiagnostic metacognitive therapy compared to disorder-specific cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety disorders: a study protocol for a randomized controlled superiority trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Anxiety disorders are common and disabling, yet only about half of patients remit after cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). This is a protocol for a pragmatic randomized controlled superiority trial comparing transdiagnostic metacognitive therapy (tMCT) with disorder-specific CBT in 86 adults with generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder or posttraumatic stress disorder in Swedish outpatient psychiatric services.
FINDINGS: The trial plans to randomize 86 adults to tMCT or CBT and follow them for 12 months. Primary outcome is self-rated principal diagnosis symptoms; secondary outcomes include clinical severity, remission, depression, functioning and quality of life. Mediation by metacognitions and cognitions will be tracked weekly, and a health economic evaluation is planned.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed but as-yet unpublished RCT protocol with clear primary and secondary endpoints and planned long-term follow-up. Its pragmatic elements enhance generalizability to routine care, but without results we cannot judge effect sizes, clinical significance or cost-effectiveness. The sample size (n=86) may be underpowered for some secondary outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No practice change is warranted until outcome data are available. Clinicians should note that this trial will provide head-to-head evidence on whether tMCT outperforms CBT and whether it is cost-effective in Swedish outpatient settings.

item.title: [12] Effect of Blonanserin on Neurotrophic Factors in Patients With Non-Responsive First-Episode Schizophrenia Treated With Early Risperidone Monotherapy-A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) examined whether switching to Blonanserin improves symptoms and neurotrophic markers in 120 adults with first-episode schizophrenia who did not respond to early Risperidone monotherapy, comparing Blonanserin with Clozapine over 3 months.
FINDINGS: After 3 months, PANSS total scores fell in both groups (mean change not reported), but the Blonanserin group showed a larger reduction (p < 0.05). Quality-of-life domains (physical, social, psychological) improved more in the Blonanserin group (p < 0.05). Serum BDNF and NRG1 increased, while S100β and NSE decreased more with Blonanserin than Clozapine (p < 0.05 for all). No serious adverse reactions were reported; most were mild and manageable.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s internal validity is limited by lack of blinding, no placebo arm, short 3-month follow-up, and absence of effect sizes or confidence intervals. The small single-center sample and post-hoc comparisons raise risks of bias. While statistically significant differences favor Blonanserin, the clinical magnitude is unclear and may not translate into meaningful functional gains. The biomarker changes are exploratory and require replication.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change practice; Clozapine remains the gold standard for treatment-resistant first-episode schizophrenia. Further large, blinded, multicenter RCTs with longer follow-up and patient-centered outcomes are needed before considering Blonanserin as an alternative.

item.title: [11] Phase-sensitive integration of motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioral therapy for anxiety disorders: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review mapped how motivational interviewing (MI) is integrated with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for anxiety disorders, aiming to improve engagement and adherence where dropout is common. Using Joanna Briggs Institute and PRISMA-ScR methods, it synthesized nine empirical studies published between 2005 and 2025.
FINDINGS: Three integration approaches were identified: pretreatment MI, concurrent/embedded MI, and intermittent/responsive MI. Studies reported improved treatment readiness, adherence, attendance, therapeutic alliance, and resistance management, but evidence for additional symptom improvement beyond standard CBT was inconsistent. Heterogeneity was high in sequencing, MI content, dosage, training, and fidelity monitoring.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (n=9), methodologically diverse, and lacks robust controlled comparisons. While MI integration shows promise for engagement and alliance, conclusions about symptom benefit are tentative. The preliminary conceptual framework may guide future research but cannot yet support firm clinical recommendations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify changing practice; MI-CBT integration may be considered cautiously to support engagement, but its incremental benefit over CBT alone remains unproven. Further rigorous trials are needed to define optimal integration strategies and patient populations.

item.title: [11] Predictive value of EEG/ECG biomarkers for treatment response in depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study investigated whether antidepressant treatment selection guided by individualized EEG/ECG biomarkers improves response rates in adults with ICD-10 depressive disorder or bipolar depression. This retrospective cohort examined four treatment modalities (ECT, rTMS, (es)ketamine, SSRIs) between 2022–2024.
FINDINGS: Among 153 patients, response rates were higher when treatment matched the biomarker report: ECT 70% vs 50%, rTMS 30% vs 13%, (es)ketamine 31% vs 10%, SSRIs 100% vs 11%. Overall, 46% (42/92) of concordant vs 26% (14/54) of non-concordant patients responded (absolute difference +20 percentage points; relative increase ≈77%; number needed to treat ≈5).
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests a potential association between biomarker-guided treatment and improved outcomes, but the retrospective design, lack of randomization, and small subgroup sizes (especially SSRIs, n=16) limit causal inference. Unmeasured confounders (e.g., baseline severity, prior treatment history) and potential selection bias in treatment assignment weaken internal validity. External validity is uncertain due to heterogeneous populations and settings. Prospective randomized trials are needed to confirm these findings and assess clinical utility.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to support routine use of EEG/ECG biomarkers for guiding antidepressant selection. Clinicians should await prospective validation before integrating these tools into practice.

item.title: [10] Training and Experiential Factors Associated With Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Referral Readiness Among Psychiatric Providers.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional survey examined psychiatric providers’ (attending psychiatrists, residents, nurse practitioners) beliefs about and readiness to refer patients for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) in treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and whether training or prior experience influenced readiness.
FINDINGS: Among 94 respondents, >90% endorsed TMS as effective (conceptual acceptance), but operational readiness varied: only 60–70% felt comfortable discussing or referring, and 40–50% knew referral pathways. Prior TMS training and having recommended TMS were associated with higher comfort, confidence, and awareness (p-values not reported). Residents had lower referral-pathway awareness than attendings. Insurance/costs were the most cited barriers, and lack of training was a common modifiable barrier.
INTERPRETATION: The study highlights a gap between conceptual acceptance and operational readiness for TMS referrals. Its cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and statistical significance is not reported, limiting certainty. Nonetheless, the pattern suggests targeted training and clearer referral workflows could improve utilization. External validity is limited to Florida providers, and self-report bias may inflate perceived competence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Training programs and services should incorporate practical TMS referral training and streamline referral pathways to enhance real-world uptake; however, these changes should be evaluated prospectively to confirm impact.

item.title: [8] Real-world clinical outcomes under intravenous and subcutaneous esketamine protocols for treatment-resistant depression: a multicenter, retrospective study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multicenter retrospective chart review compared intravenous (IV) and subcutaneous (SC) esketamine for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) in 72 Brazilian outpatients (aged 18–65) across three advanced-care centers, assessing efficacy (BDI-II) and tolerability at shared and protocol-specific endpoints.
FINDINGS: After six sessions, IV esketamine showed a numerically higher BDI-II response (OR 3.06, 95% CI 1.22–8.00; p = 0.059), though not statistically significant. At protocol-specific endpoints (IV: 6 sessions; SC: 12 sessions), categorical response did not differ (OR 1.44, 95% CI 0.57–3.73; p = 0.541). Dissociation was more frequent with IV (53.8% vs. 13.0%; p = 0.001), while nausea and BP increases were similar.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s retrospective design and modest sample size limit causal inference; unmeasured confounders (e.g., baseline severity, concurrent therapies) may bias results. The trend favoring IV at 6 sessions could reflect earlier exposure or protocol differences rather than route efficacy. SC’s comparable outcomes at 12 sessions suggest non-inferiority but require confirmation in prospective trials. Dissociation’s higher incidence with IV may guide route selection based on tolerability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SC esketamine may be a pragmatic alternative where IV access is limited, but clinicians should weigh speed of response (IV) against tolerability (SC) and operational feasibility. Findings are preliminary; shared decision-making with patients is warranted until higher-quality evidence emerges.

item.title: [6] Identification of fluid endocannabinoid and sphingolipid biomarkers in schizophrenia. A machine learning approach toward clinical value.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether lipid biomarkers in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and serum—specifically endocannabinoids and sphingolipids—can distinguish antipsychotic-naïve and treated schizophrenia patients from healthy volunteers using machine learning. The aim was to identify objective, minimally invasive biomarkers to aid schizophrenia diagnosis and monitoring.
FINDINGS: The machine learning model (IDEARS) achieved high discrimination between groups, with CSF area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.87 for antipsychotic-naïve and 0.94 for treated patients, and serum AUC values of 0.87 and 0.90, respectively. Anandamide was significantly elevated in CSF of antipsychotic-naïve patients (q = 0.010) and identified as a top serum feature. Elevated sphingadiene (d18:2) sphingolipids were conserved across CSF and serum in antipsychotic-naïve patients (q < 0.05). Treatment-specific ceramide patterns were also observed, with elevated C16–C18 and reduced long-chain (>C24) species in treated patients.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed exploratory study using advanced mass spectrometry and machine learning in a relatively small but carefully matched cohort (n = 49–56 per group). The high AUC values suggest potential diagnostic utility, but the study is limited by its cross-sectional design, lack of external validation, and absence of clinical outcome data. The findings are biologically plausible given known roles of the endocannabinoid and sphingolipid systems in schizophrenia, but clinical applicability remains uncertain until replicated in larger, diverse populations and linked to functional or diagnostic endpoints.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results support further investigation into lipid biomarkers for schizophrenia, particularly anandamide and sphingolipid species, as potential adjuncts to diagnosis or treatment monitoring. However, routine use is not yet justified; larger prospective studies with clinical follow-up are needed before considering integration into psychiatric practice.

item.title: [6] Association between Multimorbidity and Suicidal Behaviors among People with Psychotic Disorders.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study examined whether multimorbidity (≥2 chronic conditions) is associated with suicidal ideation and behaviors in 748 adults with psychotic disorders (e.g., schizophrenia), a group with high premature mortality.
FINDINGS: In adjusted models, multimorbidity was linked to higher odds of suicidal ideation (OR 2.31, 95% CI 1.61–3.32) and suicidal behaviors (OR 1.84, 95% CI 1.15–2.97). Results were similar in a subgroup with early psychosis (≤30 years) and when only physical multimorbidity was considered.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; temporality between multimorbidity and suicidality cannot be established. Confounding by unmeasured factors (e.g., substance use, medication side-effects) remains possible. The effect sizes are moderate but clinically plausible; however, replication in longitudinal cohorts is needed before practice changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports screening for suicidality in psychotic patients with multimorbidity, but does not yet justify multimorbidity-specific suicide-prevention interventions without further study.

item.title: [6] Neuroanatomical Subtypes of Schizophrenia Reveal Divergent Atrophy Trajectories and Distinct Associations with Long-Term Clozapine Use.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This longitudinal cohort study (6-year follow-up) used MRI-based subtyping to explore heterogeneity in brain atrophy trajectories among patients with schizophrenia (n=467) from the Genetic Risk and Outcome of Psychosis cohort, aiming to link neuroanatomical subtypes to long-term clozapine use and molecular signatures.
FINDINGS: Two neuroanatomical subtypes emerged: subtype 1 (65.5%) with widespread cortical volume loss at baseline and stable decline over 6 years, and subtype 2 (34.5%) with hippocampal/amygdala volume loss at baseline but accelerated atrophy over time. Subtype 1 had significantly higher clozapine use than subtype 2 (36% vs. 17%; χ² = 5.62, P = 0.02). Atrophy patterns in subtype 1 mirrored those observed in clozapine users, and subtypes showed divergent associations with neurotransmitter density and schizophrenia-related gene expression maps.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence for biologically distinct schizophrenia subtypes with divergent atrophy trajectories and differential clozapine exposure. However, the observational design precludes causal inference, and the modest sample size (n=467) limits generalisability. The statistical significance (P=0.02) is modest, and clinical significance remains uncertain without direct outcome data (e.g., symptom improvement or side effects). The molecular associations are hypothesis-generating and require replication.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This subtyping framework may eventually inform stratified treatment approaches, but current evidence is insufficient to guide clozapine prescribing. Clinicians should await further validation before considering neuroanatomical subtypes in routine care.

item.title: [6] Rapid antidepressant effects of ketamine combined with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors: Mechanisms and outlook.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether combining ketamine with SSRIs produces faster or greater antidepressant effects than SSRIs alone in MDD, and explores proposed mechanisms (GLIMPSE model) and safety monitoring. It synthesizes prior clinical observations and preclinical data rather than testing a new intervention.
FINDINGS: The authors cite prior open-label and small controlled studies suggesting that a single subanesthetic ketamine dose can accelerate SSRI response and improve residual symptoms, but they do not report new quantitative effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values. They propose a mechanistic model (GLIMPSE) linking dorsal raphe–prefrontal 5-HT–glutamate/GABA circuits to synaptic metaplasticity and outline a serotonin syndrome safety protocol.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review without original data, the strength of evidence is low. The proposed GLIMPSE model is speculative and not yet empirically validated. The safety protocol is reasonable but not evidence-based for this specific combination. The clinical observations summarized are preliminary and heterogeneous, so conclusions about efficacy remain uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine use of ketamine–SSRI combinations outside research settings. Clinicians should await adequately powered RCTs with clear safety monitoring before considering this approach.

item.title: [19] [Meeting the growing needs for CBT for psychosis: An innovative, clinically-oriented online training program].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study describes the development and structure of an innovative 45-hour online French-language training program for cognitive behavioral therapy for psychosis (CBTp), designed to address the insufficient accessibility of CBTp in French-speaking settings. The program targets both future and practicing mental health professionals, aiming to enhance knowledge, attitudes, and clinical skills through asynchronous and blended learning formats.
FINDINGS: The program consists of three components: (1) a fully asynchronous, self-paced module on core CBTp skills; (2) a blended module introducing group-based CBTp with synchronous sessions, role-plays, and supervision; and (3) a blended module addressing clinical complexity in individual CBTp with similar interactive elements. The program integrates narrated slide presentations, formative self-assessments, and summative evaluations for accreditation, with the goal of improving accessibility and quality of psychosis care.
INTERPRETATION: This is a descriptive study outlining a training program rather than a clinical trial, so no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported. The strengths include its comprehensive, multi-component design and focus on both theoretical and practical skills. However, the lack of outcome data (e.g., participant competence, patient outcomes, or program efficacy) limits conclusions about its effectiveness. External validity is uncertain, as the program’s impact on clinical practice and patient care remains untested.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This program may improve access to CBTp training in French-speaking regions, but its clinical impact is unproven. Clinicians should await empirical evaluation of its effectiveness before assuming it will enhance psychosis care.

item.title: [17] Mental Health Promotion in Victims of Colombian Armed Conflict: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study explores mental health promotion interventions for victims of the Colombian armed conflict, addressing a critical public health need. It uses a scoping review design to synthesize evidence from diverse sources, including clinical trials, qualitative research, and government reports.
FINDINGS: Out of 317 initial records, only six studies met inclusion criteria after rigorous screening. Two randomized clinical trials (RCTs) reported improvements in depression, anxiety, and PTSD symptoms, while one study assessed functionality impairments. However, methodological limitations such as sample loss, population heterogeneity, and non-standardized scales were noted.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is very small (only two RCTs) and heterogeneous, limiting strong conclusions. The methodological flaws (e.g., lack of standardized tools, high dropout) reduce internal validity. External validity is also constrained by diverse populations and settings. The findings are preliminary and suggest a need for larger, well-designed trials with standardized outcome measures.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not yet justify widespread adoption of specific mental health promotion interventions for conflict victims in Colombia. Clinicians should remain cautious and prioritize evidence-based trauma-focused therapies until higher-quality studies confirm benefits.

item.title: [16] Cancer risk among individuals with mental illness - a systematic review and meta-analysis of nordic register-based prospective studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether individuals with mental illness in Nordic countries have a higher-than-expected risk of developing cancer, using nationwide register-based prospective data. The study addressed a gap in understanding cancer risk in psychiatric populations, synthesizing evidence from multiple Nordic cohorts.
FINDINGS: Meta-analyses found no overall association between schizophrenia and cancer risk (heterogeneous data), but identified increased breast cancer risk (pooled SIR: 1.28, 95% CI: 1.08–1.52) and reduced risks of rectal (SIR: 0.75, 95% CI: 0.59–0.95) and prostate cancer (SIR: 0.53, 95% CI: 0.48–0.59). Mood, anxiety, and stress-related disorders, as well as autism and intellectual disability, showed higher overall cancer risk in some studies, though results varied by cancer type and sex.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength due to heterogeneity, particularly for schizophrenia, and reliance on registry data with potential unmeasured confounders (e.g., lifestyle, medication). While some associations (e.g., breast cancer in schizophrenia) are statistically significant, effect sizes are modest, and clinical significance remains uncertain. The lack of consistent patterns across mental disorders and cancer types limits firm conclusions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify routine cancer screening changes for psychiatric patients but highlight the need for vigilance in high-risk groups (e.g., schizophrenia with breast cancer risk). Further research should explore mechanisms (e.g., biological, behavioral, or healthcare access factors) to inform targeted prevention strategies.

item.title: [16] [Update of the S3 guidelines "Screening, diagnosis, and treatment of alcohol-use disorders"].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The 2024 update of the German S3 guideline on alcohol-use disorders (AUD) revises diagnostic criteria and care pathways to align with ICD-11 and incorporates evidence on comorbidities and special populations. It is a structured consensus guideline intended to standardise care across psychiatric and addiction services.
FINDINGS: The revision introduces more precise ICD-11–aligned diagnostic criteria, expands sections on somatic and psychiatric comorbidities, and adds differentiated recommendations for pregnant women, children/adolescents, older adults, family members, and gender/diversity-sensitive care. It outlines a structured care pathway from screening through withdrawal, post-acute treatment, rehabilitation, and relapse prevention, with emphasis on cross-sectoral coordination.
INTERPRETATION: As a guideline update rather than a primary research study, its strength lies in synthesising current evidence and expert consensus to improve standardisation and comprehensiveness of AUD care. Limitations include reliance on consensus where high-quality evidence is sparse and potential regional variability in implementation. The clinical impact depends on local adoption and resource availability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should adopt the updated diagnostic criteria and structured care pathways, paying special attention to comorbidity screening and tailored interventions for vulnerable groups. Implementation may require system-level changes in service coordination.

item.title: [14] ED Initiated Buprenorphine and Outpatient Referrals for Opioid Use: A Literature Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review assessed whether initiating buprenorphine in the emergency department (ED) for adults with opioid use disorder, combined with referral, improves short-term outcomes. Eight heterogeneous studies (RCTs, cohorts, guidelines, implementation research) were synthesized to examine treatment engagement, illicit opioid use, withdrawal, relapse, and ED revisits.
FINDINGS: Across included studies, ED-initiated buprenorphine with referral consistently increased outpatient treatment engagement (no pooled effect size reported). Patients reported reduced withdrawal symptoms and lower relapse rates post-discharge compared with usual care or delayed referral. Repeat ED visits were not consistently reduced. No major safety signals were identified.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous (study designs, comparators, and outcomes vary), limiting firm conclusions. The lack of meta-analytic pooling and standardized effect sizes precludes precise estimates of benefit. While the direction of effect is consistent, the strength of evidence is moderate due to risk of bias in non-randomized designs and potential publication bias. Clinically, the intervention appears promising but requires more robust trials to confirm effect size and durability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: ED-initiated buprenorphine with referral may improve short-term treatment engagement and reduce withdrawal and relapse, but current evidence is not definitive. Implementation should proceed cautiously with attention to local resources and follow-up pathways until higher-quality data are available.

item.title: [13] Pathways to medication adherence: a configurational analysis of psychiatric symptoms and medication attitude in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder receiving long-acting injectable antipsychotics.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This secondary analysis (cmQCA) of 304 Italian patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder on long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics examined how combinations of psychiatric symptoms influence adherence via medication attitudes. The study aimed to identify symptom patterns that promote or hinder adherence in real-world LAI treatment.
FINDINGS: QCA identified six symptom configurations: three associated with positive medication attitudes (46% solution coverage, 82% consistency) and three linked to poor attitudes (39.5% coverage, 79.4% consistency), with high *Resistance* emerging as a key negative factor. Regression models confirmed partial mediation through medication attitudes (DAI-10), while controlling for demographics, substance use, LAI type, and injection interval.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is exploratory (cmQCA is a qualitative method) and relies on a single-country sample with cross-sectional data, limiting causal inference. The identified symptom patterns (e.g., absence of positive symptoms and resistance) suggest potential targets for adherence interventions, but replication in prospective studies is needed. The small effect sizes and lack of clinical adherence thresholds weaken claims of direct clinical impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians may consider assessing symptom profiles (e.g., high resistance) and medication attitudes in LAI-treated patients to guide adherence support, but this study does not yet provide actionable thresholds or validated interventions.

item.title: [12] Rosie en Español, a Chatbot-Delivered Intervention for Spanish-Speaking, US-Based Latina Mothers: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This pilot RCT tested "Rosie," a Spanish-language AI chatbot for perinatal Latina mothers in the US, against a book-club control to assess feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary mental health effects on depression, anxiety, and stress over 3 months.
FINDINGS: 30 participants were randomized 1:1; baseline scores were low. Within the Rosie group, anxiety decreased from mean 3.27 (SD 2.89) to 1.27 (SD 2.94; P=.02) and perceived stress from 30.00 (SD 5.53) to 17.80 (SD 12.99; P=.003). Depression fell modestly in both arms. No between-group differences reached significance, and healthcare-use measures were unchanged. Engagement and qualitative feedback were positive.
INTERPRETATION: The study shows feasibility and high acceptability but is underpowered for between-group comparisons; observed within-group improvements may reflect regression to the mean or placebo effects. The lack of control-group superiority and small sample limit internal validity. Larger, adequately powered trials are needed to confirm effectiveness and assess clinical significance.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify changing practice; Rosie may be a promising adjunct, but efficacy remains unproven. Clinicians should await larger trials before recommending it as a replacement for standard perinatal mental health care.

item.title: [10] Prevalence and associated factors of suicidal ideation, suicide plans, and suicide attempts among nurses: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (55 studies, 18 countries) estimated the pooled prevalence of suicidal ideation (SI) and suicide plans (SP) among nurses and explored associated factors, addressing a gap in occupational mental health evidence.
FINDINGS: The pooled prevalence of SI was 12.8% (95% CI: 10.1–15.7; 95% PI: 3.2–36.3; I² = 99.0%) and for SP was 5.0% (95% CI: 3.8–6.4; 95% PI: 1.6–17.6; I² = 70.2%). Subgroup analyses showed variation by country (e.g., 6.1% in Spain to 15.5% in Ireland), region (highest in Asia: 15.7%), and recall period (highest for past-week: 18.1%). Meta-regression suggested younger mean age was associated with higher SI prevalence (R² = 25.86%).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is large but highly heterogeneous (I² > 90% for SI), limiting precision of pooled estimates. Wide prediction intervals indicate that prevalence varies substantially across settings and populations. While psychological and occupational factors are frequently implicated, causal inference is limited by cross-sectional designs and narrative synthesis of associated factors. The findings underscore occupational risks but should be interpreted cautiously due to methodological variability and potential publication bias (Egger’s test mentioned but not reported in detail).
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These results suggest that suicidal ideation and plans are not rare among nurses, supporting the need for routine screening in occupational health settings. However, the heterogeneity and lack of longitudinal data preclude firm recommendations on specific interventions; workplace mental health programs should be implemented with monitoring for local context and risk factors.

item.title: [9] Neurocomputational training to boost reward learning and sensitivity in anhedonic individuals: a transdiagnostic proof-of-concept trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether a novel reward-learning (RL) training could improve reward sensitivity and learning in 50 anhedonic individuals with depression and/or anxiety, using a randomized controlled trial (RCT) design with sham comparator and neuroimaging outcomes.
FINDINGS: Participants in the active RL training showed greater increases in reward maximization (effect size not reported) and reduced anterior cingulate cortex activation to reward prediction errors compared to sham. Exploratory mediation analyses suggested that improved reward maximization during training was linked to increased positive affect in the active group.
INTERPRETATION: The RCT provides preliminary evidence that RL training may enhance reward learning and neural efficiency in anhedonic individuals, but effect sizes and clinical significance are unclear. The study is limited by small sample size, lack of long-term follow-up, and exploratory mediation analyses. External validity is uncertain due to the highly selected sample (e.g., transdiagnostic but excluding severe comorbidities).
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This proof-of-concept trial suggests potential for computerized RL training to target anhedonia, but routine use is premature. Further trials with larger samples, clinical outcomes, and real-world transfer are needed before considering integration into practice.

item.title: [9] [Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical decision support systems for suicide risk assessment in emergency departments using Quebec health administrative data].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores the potential of AI-enabled clinical decision support systems (CDSS) for suicide risk assessment in emergency departments using Quebec’s health administrative data, focusing on their role as adjuncts to—not replacements for—clinical judgment. It highlights ethical, organizational, and clinical challenges in implementing such systems.
FINDINGS: The review emphasizes that while AI models may improve population-level risk stratification, their accuracy for *individual* suicide prediction remains limited. Key concerns include algorithmic opacity, risk of bias in training data, and challenges in clinical integration. The authors argue for transparent governance, clinician training, and patient partnership in development and implementation.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence presented is preliminary and theoretical, based on a narrative review rather than empirical data. The authors acknowledge the lack of robust validation for individual-level prediction and call for prospective studies to assess clinical effectiveness, acceptability, and implementation feasibility. The discussion of ethical and practical challenges is thorough but not quantified.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current AI tools should not replace clinical judgment but may serve as supplementary aids in suicide risk assessment. Clinicians should await prospective validation studies before considering adoption, ensuring systems are transparent, equitable, and integrated with patient-centered care.

item.title: [9] Effects of different doses of esketamine as an adjunct to sufentanil-based patient-controlled intravenous analgesia on postoperative analgesia and opioid consumption following lumbar decompression surgery: a dose-finding randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind, dose-finding RCT (n=120) tested whether adding esketamine to sufentanil-based patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) after lumbar decompression surgery improves postoperative pain control and reduces opioid use, and which dose gives the best risk–benefit profile.
FINDINGS: All esketamine groups (0.25, 0.5, 1.0 mg/kg) had lower VAS pain scores at all time points and reduced 24-h sufentanil consumption vs control (P<0.05), with no significant differences among esketamine doses. Ramsay sedation scores rose dose-dependently (S3 > S2 > S1), and the 1.0 mg/kg group showed more hypotension and dissociative symptoms. Oxidative-stress markers improved in all esketamine groups.
INTERPRETATION: The trial is internally valid (randomized, double-blind, clear dosing strata) but limited by short-term, single-surgery follow-up and lack of placebo control for esketamine. The analgesic benefit plateaus across doses while adverse effects increase, suggesting a ceiling effect. The 0.25 mg/kg dose appears to offer the best balance, but longer-term safety and psychiatric outcomes were not assessed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For post-lumbar decompression analgesia, adding low-dose esketamine (≈0.25 mg/kg) to a reduced sufentanil PCIA regimen can improve pain control and cut opioid use, but clinicians should monitor sedation, blood pressure, and dissociative symptoms, especially at higher doses.

item.title: [8] Unhealthy Alcohol Use in People Living with HIV: A Narrative Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review synthesizes evidence on the epidemiology, mechanisms, and interventions for unhealthy alcohol use (UAU) in people living with HIV (PLWH), a syndemic relationship that worsens HIV treatment outcomes. It highlights gaps in screening and treatment despite high UAU prevalence.
FINDINGS: UAU in PLWH is associated with reduced ART adherence, lower viral suppression, and increased mortality. Structural barriers (e.g., poverty, stigma) and behavioral factors (e.g., intentional ART skipping) exacerbate poor outcomes. Promising interventions (e.g., naltrexone, motivational interviewing, cash transfers) are underutilized due to inconsistent implementation and provider hesitancy.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study lacks quantitative synthesis or rigorous methodological appraisal, limiting confidence in its conclusions. Strengths include broad coverage of mechanisms and interventions, but heterogeneity in evidence and absence of effect sizes or confidence intervals weaken internal validity. External validity is constrained by reliance on selected studies rather than systematic inclusion. The clinical urgency is clear, but specific recommendations remain tentative without stronger evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritize UAU screening in PLWH using validated tools (e.g., AUDIT-C) and consider integrating behavioral and pharmacologic interventions where appropriate. Structural barriers (e.g., stigma, poverty) must be addressed alongside clinical care, though evidence for optimal intervention combinations remains preliminary.

item.title: [7] Levodopa or dopamine agonists for enhancing motor function after stroke.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Cochrane systematic review assessed whether levodopa or dopamine agonists improve motor function after stroke in adults, using data from 12 randomised controlled trials (n=1860) published up to November 2025.
FINDINGS: Across six trials (1258 participants), continuous motor function scores showed no difference between dopaminergic agents and comparators (SMD 1.42, 95% CI -0.20 to 3.05; very low-certainty evidence). Two trials (615 participants) found no difference in dichotomous motor outcomes (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82–1.06; low-certainty evidence). Serious adverse events were similar between groups (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.83–1.27; low-certainty evidence). A sensitivity analysis of two low-risk-of-bias trials (n=1025) confirmed no effect (SMD 0.02, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.14).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is very low to low certainty due to heterogeneity, imprecision, and risk-of-bias concerns. The wide CIs and null findings across outcomes suggest no clinically meaningful benefit of levodopa or dopamine agonists for post-stroke motor recovery. Subgroup effects remain untested.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support using levodopa or dopamine agonists to enhance motor recovery after stroke; further targeted trials are needed before any practice change.

item.title: [32] Lithium in the Prevention of Postpartum Recurrence of Mood Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The clinical question is whether prophylactic lithium reduces postpartum relapse in women with bipolar disorder (BD-I or BD-II) compared to no lithium. This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO registered) synthesised observational studies and small comparative cohorts to address a high-risk period for recurrence.
FINDINGS: Eight studies (n=554) contributed to the main analysis. The pooled postpartum recurrence proportion was 21 % (95 % CI 15–29 %) with lithium versus 41 % (95 % CI 33–50 %) without lithium. Two additional studies showed higher relapse after lithium discontinuation, but these were indirect comparisons.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small, observational, and at risk of confounding by indication (sicker patients may stay on lithium). Heterogeneity and limited data on dosing, serum levels, and neonatal outcomes further weaken certainty. The absolute risk reduction (~20 %) is potentially meaningful, but the pooled estimate is driven by non-randomised designs with unclear adjustment for confounders.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Lithium may lower postpartum recurrence risk, yet the strength of evidence is low; shared decision-making and close monitoring are essential, especially given neonatal risks. Larger, well-controlled prospective studies are needed before firm practice recommendations can be made.

item.title: [20] The overall effects of virtual reality interventions on ICU patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO-registered) evaluated whether virtual reality (VR) interventions improve psychological distress, pain, sleep, functional outcomes, or delirium in adult ICU patients, synthesizing 20 RCTs (n=1551) published 2000–2025.
FINDINGS: VR reduced anxiety (SMD −0.67, 95 % CI −1.00 to −0.35), depression (SMD −0.46, 95 % CI −0.72 to −0.21), PTSD symptoms (mean difference −5.48, 95 % CI −9.36 to −1.59), improved sleep quality (SMD 0.70, 95 % CI 0.47–0.92) and lower-limb function (mean difference 2.83, 95 % CI 1.99–3.67). No significant effect was found for pain (SMD −0.57, 95 % CI −1.49 to 0.36) or bedside balance (SMD 0.61, 95 % CI −0.44 to 1.66).
INTERPRETATION: Evidence quality was rated very low to moderate, with most trials at unclear or high risk of bias. Effect sizes for anxiety and sleep are moderate and potentially clinically meaningful, whereas depression and PTSD effects are smaller. Pain and balance outcomes remain uncertain. Larger, rigorously designed RCTs with standardized VR protocols and objective outcome measures are needed before firm clinical recommendations can be made.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current data suggest VR may be a useful adjunct for anxiety and sleep disturbance in ICU patients, but evidence for pain relief and motor recovery is insufficient; implementation should await higher-quality trials.

item.title: [13] Clozapine Augmentation Strategies and Clinical Predictors of Prolonged Tertiary Hospitalization in Clozapine-Resistant Schizophrenia: a Retrospective Cohort Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study (2012–2025) examined augmentation strategies (aripiprazole, amisulpride, ECT) in 88 inpatients with clozapine-resistant schizophrenia (CRS) and their association with length of stay (LOS) and symptom change.
FINDINGS: In adjusted Cox models, amisulpride (D2/3R selective antagonist) at index was linked to shorter LOS vs ECT (HR 2.50, 95% CI 1.35–4.62); aripiprazole (partial agonist) was not (HR 1.41, 95% CI 0.75–2.63). At discharge, ECT produced greater reductions in positive symptoms than amisulpride (MD −3.20, 95% CI −5.65 to −0.75) and aripiprazole (MD −3.87, 95% CI −6.57 to −1.16). Baseline severe psychosis and functional impairment predicted ECT use (AUC 0.74).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by its retrospective design, small sample, and single-centre setting, which constrain causal inference and generalisability. The observed LOS advantage for amisulpride and symptom gains with ECT are statistically significant but modest in magnitude; clinical significance remains uncertain without corroboration from larger, prospective studies. Confounding by indication and unmeasured variables (e.g., prior treatment response) may bias estimates.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest amisulpride may shorten hospitalisation and ECT may yield greater positive-symptom improvement in CRS, but selection should be individualised and guided by baseline severity; robust RCTs are needed before practice changes.

item.title: [11] Prefrontal Cortical Changes With Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement in Opioid Use Disorder: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This randomized clinical trial (RCT) examined whether Mindfulness-Oriented Recovery Enhancement (MORE) alters prefrontal cortical activity in individuals with opioid use disorder (OUD) and whether such changes relate to clinical outcomes like craving and abstinence duration. Conducted in an inpatient rehabilitation setting in New York, 59 adults with OUD were randomized to MORE or psychoeducational supportive therapy (PST), with neuroimaging and clinical outcomes assessed over 8 weeks and at ~4-month follow-up.
FINDINGS: In fMRI analyses, MORE reduced drug-biased activity in the middle frontal gyrus and precuneus during downregulation of drug cues compared with PST (z > 3.1; P < .05). Shifts from drug to natural reward responses in lateral and ventromedial prefrontal cortex were associated with lower cue-induced craving only in the MORE group (z > 3.1; P < .05). MORE also reduced medial prefrontal synchronization to drug-related movie scenes (q = 0.019) and extended abstinence duration at follow-up (χ² = 6.7; P = .04; Cohen w = 0.19).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary evidence that MORE may modulate prefrontal cortical networks involved in reward processing and craving regulation in OUD. However, the small sample size (n = 59), limited follow-up duration (~4 months), and modest effect size for abstinence (Cohen w = 0.19) temper conclusions. The neuroimaging findings are biologically plausible but require replication in larger, more diverse samples with longer follow-up to determine clinical significance and generalizability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MORE may serve as a useful adjunct to standard OUD treatments by targeting neural mechanisms of craving, but current evidence does not yet justify replacing established pharmacotherapies. Clinicians should consider MORE as a complementary intervention while awaiting larger, longer-term trials to confirm durability of effects.

item.title: [10] Energetic metabolism in bipolar disorder: from markers to precision therapeutics.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examines whether mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and metabolic disturbances contribute to bipolar disorder (BD) pathophysiology and whether these mechanisms could guide precision therapeutics. It synthesises human neuroimaging, peripheral biomarker, and intervention studies identified via PRISMA-guided searches.
FINDINGS: Across included studies, BD was associated with impaired oxidative phosphorylation, reduced ATP and phosphocreatine, altered NAD+/NADH ratios, elevated lactate, and decreased tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediates on neuroimaging. Peripheral markers showed decreased electron transport chain complex activity, increased oxidative damage (MDA, 8-OHdG), altered purinergic enzymes, and elevated mitochondrial DNA. Small trials of mitochondrial cofactors (creatine, CoQ10, carnitine, NAC) and metabolic strategies (ketogenic diet) reported signals of benefit, but sample sizes were small and heterogeneity high.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is largely observational and heterogeneous, limiting causal inference. Biomarker abnormalities are consistent but not specific to BD, and intervention trials are preliminary with unclear clinical significance. Funding sources and risk of bias were not reported in the abstract, so external validity and internal validity remain uncertain. Large, standardised, multicentre RCTs are needed before any biomarker-guided stratification or metabolic intervention can be recommended.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, routine metabolic or mitochondrial testing cannot be justified for BD management. Clinicians should remain alert to emerging data but avoid adopting unproven metabolic interventions outside research settings.

item.title: [10] Semaglutide and Panic Attacks: Active-Comparator Disproportionality Analysis, Temporal Assessment of Notoriety Bias and Evidence Triangulation in Post-Marketing Pharmacovigilance.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether reports of panic attacks linked to semaglutide in the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) reflect a true drug-related signal or biases such as confounding by indication and notoriety bias. It used an active-comparator disproportionality analysis and triangulated findings with published evidence from randomized and observational studies.
FINDINGS: Among 33,267 semaglutide reports, panic attacks were reported in 0.26% (87 cases), compared to 0.05% (28) with dulaglutide and 0.05% (13) with empagliflozin. Crude reporting odds ratios (RORs) for semaglutide vs. comparators were ~5.0, but adjusted RORs (aRORs) fell to ~2.8. Temporal analyses showed the crude RORs were lower before July 2023 (aROR ~1.3) and rose sharply afterward (42.0 panic reports per 10,000 semaglutide reports in 2023–2024 vs. 6.7 in 2018–2022; p = 0.007). Across 12 studies, no consistent increase in panic or anxiety outcomes was found with semaglutide.
INTERPRETATION: The initial signal of semaglutide-associated panic attacks in FAERS was largely driven by confounding and notoriety bias, especially after a regulatory communication in mid-2023. The adjusted analyses and lack of consistent findings in clinical studies weaken any causal inference. The study demonstrates the value of active-comparator designs and temporal bias assessment in pharmacovigilance, but disproportionality analyses remain hypothesis-generating.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support a clinically meaningful association between semaglutide and panic attacks. Clinicians should remain alert to anxiety symptoms in patients using GLP-1 receptor agonists but not attribute them to the drug without further evaluation.

item.title: [9] Efficacy of Personalizing Cognitive Remediation for Schizophrenia by Targeting Impairments in Early Auditory Processing.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether adding early auditory processing (EAP) training to cognitive remediation (CR) in outpatients with schizophrenia would yield greater cognitive or functional gains in those with baseline EAP deficits (EAP–) than in those without (EAP+). It was a confirmatory randomized trial (n=184) comparing CR with vs without EAP modules, with follow-up at 3 months.
FINDINGS: The overall cognitive gain effect size was moderate (≈0.5) across both treatment arms. There was no significant between-group difference in EAP, cognitive or functional outcomes at endpoint for either EAP– or EAP+ patients. EAP improved modestly (small effect size) in EAP– patients regardless of module assignment. Cognitive gains did not mediate the relationship between EAP gains and functional capacity.
INTERPRETATION: The trial provides moderate-quality evidence that personalizing CR by adding EAP training does not confer additional benefit over standard CR for either EAP– or EAP+ patients. Strengths include the randomized design and 3-month follow-up; weaknesses include lack of an active control and modest observed effects. The small improvements in EAP across conditions suggest some malleability of EAP, but the absence of differential gains limits clinical utility of personalization based on baseline EAP status.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, routine addition of EAP-specific modules to CR for schizophrenia cannot be justified on efficacy grounds. Standard CR remains valuable, but tailoring by EAP status does not appear to enhance outcomes.

item.title: [9] Remission Trajectories During Low-Intensity Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A 2-Year Naturalistic Follow-Up Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This prospective cohort study examined 2-year remission trajectories in adults with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) receiving low-intensity cognitive behavioural therapy (LiCBT) in routine outpatient care, addressing a gap in evidence on longer-term outcomes beyond short-term high-intensity CBT protocols.
FINDINGS: Of 62 eligible patients, 47 completed 2-year follow-up. Remission occurred in 18 patients at 1 year and an additional 10 by 2 years. Baseline Y-BOCS scores were lower in the early remission group than in the non-remission group (mean difference not reported). By 1 year, Y-BOCS scores differed significantly across early remission, delayed remission, and non-remission groups (p-value not reported).
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests heterogeneous remission trajectories over two years, with some patients remitting later than others. However, the lack of reported effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values limits precision. The small sample (n=47 completers) and single-centre design reduce generalisability. The naturalistic setting enhances external validity for routine care but introduces confounding from adjunctive treatments. The clinical significance of delayed remission remains uncertain without data on functional outcomes or relapse rates.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider that remission may occur beyond the first year in some OCD patients receiving LiCBT, supporting ongoing monitoring rather than early discontinuation. However, the evidence is preliminary and does not yet justify changing standard follow-up intervals.

item.title: [8] Global Burden of Anorexia Nervosa and Bulimia Nervosa, 1990 to 2023, With Forecasts to 2050: A Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 analysis estimated the global prevalence, disability burden (YLDs, DALYs), and mortality of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa from 1990 to 2023, with forecasts to 2050, using data from 204 countries. The study addresses the public health significance of these eating disorders as major causes of nonfatal mental health burden.
FINDINGS: In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people (95% UI: 13.9–24.0) globally had anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa, with 69.4% being female. These cases accounted for 3.83 million DALYs (95% UI: 2.23–5.69). Since 1990, global prevalent cases increased by 71.0%, while age-standardized prevalence and DALY rates rose by ~21%. High-income regions (e.g., Australasia, Western Europe) had the highest prevalence, but the largest relative increases occurred in East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia. Forecasts predict continued increases in prevalent cases through 2050.
INTERPRETATION: The GBD 2023 study provides robust global estimates using a standardized methodology across 204 countries, enhancing comparability. However, reliance on modeled data from heterogeneous sources (surveys, registries) introduces uncertainty, particularly in regions with sparse data. The observed increases may reflect improved detection or true rising incidence, but disentangling these is challenging. The clinical significance of the modest age-standardized rate increases (~21%) is unclear, though the absolute burden (3.83 million DALYs) underscores the need for public health attention. The forecasted growth highlights urgency for prevention and service planning.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support integrating eating disorders into global mental health surveillance and resource allocation. Clinicians should anticipate rising demand for services, particularly in regions with rapid increases, and prioritize early detection and intervention, especially among adolescents and young adults.

item.title: [8] C-Reactive Protein Levels and Elevations in Schizophrenia: The Central Role of Body Mass Index.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study examined whether elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) levels in individuals with schizophrenia are primarily driven by body mass index (BMI) or other factors, using 772 participants (479 with schizophrenia, 293 controls) and sequential regression models.
FINDINGS: Schizophrenia was associated with higher CRP (P < .001) after adjusting for sex, age, maternal education, race, and smoking. Adding BMI attenuated but did not eliminate the group difference (still P < .001). Within the schizophrenia group, BMI was the strongest predictor of CRP (β = +0.031 per unit increase, P < .001), explaining a substantial portion of CRP variance. Only 7 of 20 initially significant clinical/medication variables remained significant after full adjustment and multiple comparison correction.
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests that BMI is a major confounder in CRP elevations observed in schizophrenia, though residual group differences persist after adjustment. Strengths include a large sample and rigorous modeling, but the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The clinical significance of the residual CRP difference remains unclear, as effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported. Funding sources and blinding status are not mentioned, which could introduce bias.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider BMI when interpreting CRP levels in schizophrenia, as obesity may drive much of the observed inflammation. However, this study does not establish whether CRP reduction improves outcomes, so routine CRP monitoring for inflammatory risk in schizophrenia remains unproven.

item.title: [6] The Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model: Health System Implementation in Wartime Ukraine.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The paper describes the implementation of a new trauma-informed mental health care model ("Unbroken Integrative Psycho-Trauma Care Model") in a civilian hospital in Lviv, Ukraine, during the ongoing war (Feb 2022–Dec 2025). It addresses the challenge of delivering large-scale, multidisciplinary mental health care amid active conflict, complex trauma, and limited guidance.
FINDINGS: Over the study period, the Lviv First Medical Union treated >15 000 war-related injuries and >400 former prisoners of war. Within this setting, 7538 unique individuals received psychiatric care, including 4165 who received trauma-focused psychotherapy. The model used proactive psychiatric rounds, structured triage into 4 clinical pathways, stabilization-first sequencing, and longitudinal case management integrated with other medical services.
INTERPRETATION: This is a descriptive Special Communication (not an empirical study), so no effect sizes, p-values, or comparative data are reported. The model’s innovation lies in its system-level organization rather than a specific intervention. While the scale and integration are impressive, the lack of formal evaluation (e.g., outcomes, comparator, or statistical analysis) limits conclusions about effectiveness or generalizability. The approach may offer valuable lessons for conflict-affected health systems, but its impact remains unproven.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This model may serve as a framework for organizing trauma care in war zones, but clinicians should await empirical validation before adopting it wholesale. The described workflow could inspire adaptations in similar settings, but routine implementation should be cautious until outcomes are rigorously assessed.

item.title: [6] Analysis and Prediction of Relapse Risk Factors in Community-Dwelling Individuals With Schizophrenia: Retrospective Cohort Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study (n=39,818) used machine learning (LightGBM) to predict hospitalization-related severe relapse in community-dwelling individuals with schizophrenia, aiming to identify key risk factors for targeted interventions.
FINDINGS: The LightGBM model achieved an AUC of 0.95, AUPRC of 0.79, recall of 0.77, precision of 0.71, and F1-score of 0.74 in the test set. SHAP analysis ranked medication persistence (23.30%), specialist-recommended medication adherence training (19.74%), and number of follow-ups (7.38%) as top predictors. Higher relapse risk correlated with medication non-adherence, frequent follow-ups, younger age, and higher education, while sustained medication use, occupational functioning, and social participation predicted lower risk.
INTERPRETATION: The model shows strong internal validity with high discriminative performance, but external validity is limited by its reliance on a single health system’s electronic records and retrospective design. The identified predictors align with clinical intuition (e.g., medication adherence), but causal inference is constrained by confounding (e.g., unmeasured socioeconomic factors). The clinical utility hinges on prospective validation and integration into routine care pathways.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: If validated, this model could support risk stratification in community mental health services, prioritizing adherence support and social reintegration for high-risk individuals. However, current evidence is preliminary—implementation should await external validation and assessment of real-world impact on relapse rates.

item.title: [35] The LAI-Oral Antipsychotic Efficacy-Effectiveness Paradox in Schizophrenia.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines why long-acting injectable (LAI) antipsychotics appear more effective in real-world observational studies than in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for schizophrenia relapse prevention, a paradox that has persisted for decades and contributes to underuse of LAIs. The paper consists of a scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) and a conceptual methodological framework proposing solutions to resolve this paradox.
FINDINGS: The paradox is primarily attributed to confounding by indication in observational studies and inadequate adherence measurement across all designs. The authors propose four methodological solutions: (1) digital adherence monitoring (e.g., ingestible sensors), (2) pharmacogenomic stratification (e.g., CYP2D6, CYP3A4, CYP2C19 phenotyping), (3) pragmatic RCTs with real-world eligibility and objective adherence endpoints, and (4) AI-supported neuroimaging (PET/fMRI) to assess dopamine receptor occupancy and functional connectivity.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and conceptual rather than empirical, as the proposed solutions are not validated findings but a framework for future research. The scoping review highlights key methodological gaps (confounding, adherence measurement) but does not resolve the paradox. The proposed AI and neuroimaging approaches are innovative but require rigorous testing. The study underscores the need for better-designed comparative effectiveness research to guide clinical decisions.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support a definitive superiority of LAIs over oral antipsychotics. Clinicians should remain cautious about overinterpreting observational findings favoring LAIs. Future research integrating digital monitoring, pharmacogenomics, and AI-driven neuroimaging may provide clearer guidance, but this is not yet actionable in routine practice.

item.title: [22] Efficacy of High-Frequency Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Therapy for Depression With Insomnia Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Based on Randomized Controlled Trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed whether high-frequency repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (HF-rTMS) targeting the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) improves symptoms of depression and insomnia in patients with comorbid depression and insomnia, synthesizing 7 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 709 participants.
FINDINGS: HF-rTMS significantly improved sleep quality (SMD 0.97, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.71, p = 0.01) and depressive symptoms (SMD 0.61, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.84, p < 0.00001). Sleep latency showed a non-significant trend toward improvement (SMD 0.50, 95% CI -0.17 to 1.18, p = 0.14). Adverse events were not significantly different between groups (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.48, p = 0.57). Substantial heterogeneity was present (I² = 91% for sleep quality), partly explained by differences in stimulation frequency and baseline antidepressant use.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is of very-low to low certainty due to substantial heterogeneity, methodological limitations, and potential biases in included RCTs. While the pooled effects suggest benefit, the wide confidence intervals and inconsistency across studies limit confidence in the magnitude of effect. The lack of blinding in some trials and variability in protocols further reduce internal validity. Confirmation with larger, well-designed RCTs is needed before firm conclusions can be drawn.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of HF-rTMS for comorbid depression and insomnia outside research settings. Clinicians should remain cautious and consider this modality only when standard treatments have failed, while awaiting higher-quality trials to clarify efficacy, optimal parameters, and patient selection.

item.title: [19] Is a ketogenic diet useful in the management of mood disorders?
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether a ketogenic diet (KD) can serve as an adjunctive treatment for mood disorders (MDs), summarizing recent randomized and prospective studies to assess efficacy and safety.
FINDINGS: The review reports that recent randomized and prospective studies suggest KD may improve depressive symptoms when used alongside standard treatments. However, potential adverse effects are noted, particularly in individuals with normal body weight or those without proper nutritional guidance. The lack of standardized KD protocols across studies complicates evidence synthesis.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and heterogeneous, with no clear consensus on KD implementation or outcomes. The review highlights the need for larger, well-powered randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with standardized protocols. Current findings are insufficient to support routine clinical use, and expert consensus on research protocols is a necessary next step before clinical guidelines can be developed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: KD cannot yet be recommended for routine use in mood disorders. Clinicians should remain cautious, monitor emerging evidence, and avoid recommending KD without proper nutritional supervision due to potential risks.

item.title: [14] A digital platform for ADHD assessment and management: stakeholder-informed development and clinical implications.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study describes the development of a digital platform to operationalise the ADMiRE clinical pathway for ADHD assessment and management in Irish CAMHS, addressing variability in care despite established standards. The focus is on stakeholder-informed design to improve scalability and reduce administrative burden.
FINDINGS: The digital platform was developed through an iterative, stakeholder-informed process involving clinicians and service stakeholders. Key features include structured referral management, standardised diagnostic and monitoring tools with automated scoring, medication and case management, longitudinal monitoring, and automated clinical documentation. The system aims to support more consistent, guideline-informed care and reduce administrative burden while improving continuity across services.
INTERPRETATION: This is a perspective piece rather than a clinical study, so no effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values are reported. The strength lies in its stakeholder-informed, iterative development process, which enhances face validity and potential acceptability in routine CAMHS settings. However, as a perspective, it lacks empirical evaluation of clinical outcomes, cost-effectiveness, or implementation barriers. The generalisability to other healthcare systems or populations remains uncertain until further research is conducted.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This digital platform may offer practical improvements in ADHD care by standardising assessment and management processes, but its clinical impact and feasibility in routine practice are unproven. Clinicians should await empirical validation before adopting this system.

item.title: [13] Anxiety and suicide risk: mechanism, timing, and clinical utility.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether anxiety symptoms or disorders add clinically useful information about suicide risk beyond what is captured by standard diagnoses or trait measures, and whether modifiable anxiety-related processes can inform prevention strategies.
FINDINGS: Across recent studies, panic disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, social anxiety disorder and PTSD show elevated suicide risk, but odds ratios attenuate after adjusting for depression and comorbidity. Within-person studies find that anxiety-related affect and rumination co-vary with suicidal thinking but rarely predict subsequent suicidal events. Several modifiable anxiety-related processes exist, yet durable reductions in suicidal outcomes have not been demonstrated.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous and largely observational, limiting causal inference. Adjustment for depression and comorbidity substantially reduces observed associations, suggesting anxiety alone is not a strong independent predictor. While modifiable processes exist, there is no proof that targeting them changes suicide risk; micro-randomized trials during acute risk periods are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current routine risk assessment should not rely on anxiety diagnoses or trait scales alone; instead, clinicians should monitor dynamic anxiety-related processes during high-risk periods, but should not expect such monitoring to reduce suicide risk until targeted interventions prove effective.

item.title: [13] Predicting olanzapine induced BMI increase using machine learning on population-based electronic health records.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Weight gain is a frequent adverse effect of olanzapine, but predicting which patients will have clinically significant BMI increase is challenging in routine care. This retrospective cohort study used population-based Danish electronic health records (EHR) to develop and test machine-learning models that predict ≥5 % BMI increase after olanzapine initiation.
FINDINGS: The best-performing model (XGBoost) predicted ≥5 % BMI increase within 30–180 days after initiation with an AUROC of 0.72 (2016–2024 data) and 0.79 (held-out 2025 data). Prediction of on-treatment BMI increase to the next available follow-up yielded AUROC 0.71 (2016–2024) but dropped to 0.61 in 2025; standardising to 30–180 days lowered AUROC to 0.64 and 0.58. A minimal-feature model performed almost as well as the full model. Key predictors were lower baseline BMI, younger age, higher olanzapine dose, historical BMI variability and prior anxiolytic prescriptions.
INTERPRETATION: The moderate discrimination (AUROC ~0.72–0.79) suggests that EHR-based models can flag patients at higher risk of olanzapine-related weight gain, but performance declined in temporally external validation, indicating potential overfitting or dataset shift.
