The identified predictors align with known risk factors, lending face validity, yet the study is observational and cannot establish causality. External validation in other health systems and prospective evaluation of clinical utility are needed before any bedside implementation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These models may help clinicians identify patients who merit closer metabolic monitoring or early lifestyle interventions when olanzapine is started, but they should not replace clinical judgment or standard monitoring protocols until further validation is completed.

item.title: [11] Time for psychiatry to seriously consider broad-spectrum micronutrients.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The article argues for considering broad-spectrum micronutrients (BSM) as a treatment option for psychological distress based on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) showing modest but positive effects on emotional regulation, irritability, and aggression. The clinical question is whether BSM should be integrated into psychiatric practice, and the population includes patients with psychological distress.
FINDINGS: The article cites RCTs where BSM demonstrated modest improvements in emotional regulation, irritability, and aggression, with effect sizes comparable to those seen with cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and antidepressants. However, no specific numerical data (e.g., effect sizes, confidence intervals, p-values, or sample sizes) are provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence presented is preliminary and lacks quantitative detail, making it difficult to assess the robustness of the findings. The claim that effect sizes are comparable to established treatments (CBT and antidepressants) is not substantiated with data in the abstract. The article does not address potential limitations such as heterogeneity in study populations, variability in micronutrient formulations, or long-term safety and efficacy. The argument for integrating BSM into practice is premature without more rigorous and detailed evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this article does not provide sufficient evidence to change clinical practice. Further high-quality RCTs with detailed reporting of outcomes and safety data are needed before BSM can be considered a viable treatment option for psychological distress. Clinicians should remain cautious and rely on evidence-based treatments with well-established efficacy and safety profiles.

item.title: [11] Personality disorder and substance use disorder: an updated review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This updated narrative review examines the comorbidity of personality disorder (PD) and substance use disorder (SUD), focusing on epidemiology, shared mechanisms, assessment, and management. It synthesizes recent evidence to inform clinical practice and research priorities.
FINDINGS: The review highlights a shift toward dimensional models (DSM-5 AMPD, ICD-11, HiTOP) and notes shared genetic, neurobiological, and environmental vulnerabilities (e.g., reward processing deficits, childhood adversity, negative affectivity, disinhibition). Digital phenotyping and machine learning are emerging tools for risk stratification. Integrated, personality-informed interventions show promise, with pharmacotherapy playing a supportive role. However, the authors emphasize the lack of robust longitudinal or interventional studies.
INTERPRETATION: As a narrative review, this study synthesizes diverse evidence but lacks the methodological rigor of a systematic review or meta-analysis. The conclusions are plausible but preliminary, given the absence of high-quality longitudinal or interventional data. The shift to dimensional frameworks is well-supported, but claims about the clinical utility of digital phenotyping and integrated interventions are based on emerging—not definitive—evidence. The review is useful for framing clinical questions but should not guide definitive practice changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider the dimensional nature of PD-SUD comorbidity and adopt integrated, personality-informed approaches where feasible. However, treatment decisions should still rely on established guidelines until stronger evidence emerges. Watch for evolving tools like digital phenotyping, but their role in routine care remains unproven.

item.title: [10] Efficacy of stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles in animal models of autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) lacks targeted therapies, and stem cell-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being explored as a potential treatment in animal models. This systematic review and meta-analysis assessed the efficacy of EVs on autistic-like behaviors and inflammatory markers in ASD animal models.
FINDINGS: Five animal studies (total sample size not specified in abstract) were included. Pooled analyses showed EV treatment improved autistic-like behaviors in the self-grooming test (P < 0.05), three-chamber social interaction test (P < 0.05), and marble burying test (P < 0.05). EV treatment also decreased proinflammatory cytokines IL-6 and IL-1β (P < 0.05). No significant effects were observed for the open field test, Morris Water Maze, TNF-α, or IL-10 (P > 0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is very preliminary, based on a small number of heterogeneous animal studies with unclear sample sizes and potential biases (e.g., lack of blinding, randomization details not specified in abstract). While statistically significant effects were reported, the clinical relevance is uncertain due to the preclinical nature of the evidence and the absence of effect sizes or confidence intervals in the abstract. Mechanistic associations (e.g., reduced IL-6 and IL-1β) are suggestive but not definitive.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This meta-analysis does not change clinical practice yet. Further high-quality preclinical studies and rigorous clinical trials are needed to confirm efficacy, safety, and mechanisms before considering EV therapy for ASD in humans.

item.title: [10] Antidepressant Discontinuation During Pregnancy and Risk of Mental Health-Related Emergencies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study (2023–2024) examined whether discontinuing SSRIs/SNRIs during pregnancy increases mental health-related emergency department (ED) visits among 1,462 privately insured patients in Pennsylvania with pre-pregnancy depression/anxiety. The clinical question is whether antidepressant continuation vs discontinuation affects acute psychiatric crises during and after pregnancy.
FINDINGS: 17.8% had no fills during pregnancy and 64.6% had a >60-day gap; most discontinuations occurred in the first trimester (44.9%). Before pregnancy, ED visit rates were similar between groups. During pregnancy, discontinuation was linked to higher mental health-related ED visits in the second month (58 vs 37/1,000, P=.027) and ninth month (59 vs 29/1,000, P<.01). Postpartum, discontinuation was associated with higher ED visits within 8 months (32 vs 21/1,000, P=.02).
INTERPRETATION: The study suggests discontinuation increases acute psychiatric care needs, but limitations include retrospective design, reliance on claims data (no symptom severity, adherence verification, or confounding by indication), and lack of adjustment for key confounders (e.g., psychotherapy, social support). The absolute risk difference is modest (about 10–30 extra ED visits per 1,000), and findings may not generalize beyond privately insured U.S. populations. Causality cannot be inferred.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These data support cautious continuation of antidepressants during pregnancy when clinically indicated, but do not mandate universal continuation. Shared decision-making should weigh risks of relapse against potential fetal exposure, with close monitoring for symptom exacerbation, especially in the first and third trimesters and early postpartum.
